title-group.article-title: Cationic antimicrobial peptide CC34 potential anticancer and apoptotic induction on cancer cells

abstract.p: To evaluate the potential of antimicrobial peptide CC34 for use as therapeutic agents for gastric cancer SGC-7901 and hepatocellular carcinoma HepG-2. In this study, the antibacterial activity and antibacterial mechanism were tested by the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) analysis, minimal bactericidal concentration (MBC) analysis, bacterial biofilm and NaCl permeability assays. Then, we assessed the hemolytic activity and cytotoxicity of CC34 for red blood cells and cancer cells, respectively. Apoptosis assay, cell cycle analysis, determination of intracellular ROS, western blot analysis caspase activity assay and ATP assay were further performed to investigate the mechanism of CC34 affected cancer cells. The novel peptide could inhibit Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, with low hemolytic activity against mouse and chicken erythrocytes. Moreover, CC34 exhibited higher inhibitory activity against biofilm formation. In addition, our data showed that CC34 significantly suppressed cell proliferation, in a dose dependent manner. CC34 induced apoptosis, induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, inhibited B-cell lymphoma-2 (Bcl-2) expression, increase B-cell lymphoma protein 2 associated X protein (Bax) expression, release of cytochrome c (Cyt C), promoted caspase-3 and − 9 activities and reduced cellular ATP levels in cancer cells. Our results indicate that CC34 with antimicrobial activity have a highly potent ability to induced apoptosis via mitochondrial-mediated apoptotic pathway in cancer cells.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) also known as host-defense peptides, are effective weapons against infections. These peptides are strongly cationic, with a net positive charge between + 2 and + 7 (Hancock et al. 2000; Margit et al. 2017). Studies have shown that AMPs have toxic to bacteria, fungi, viruses and tumor cells (Shagaghi et al. 2016). The bactericidal mechanism of AMPs can be divided into two major types models. Antimicrobial peptides can change intracellular osmotic pressure by destroying bacterial membrane. These models include barrel stave model, carpet model and toroidal pore model (Bocchinfuso et al. 2009). Another way of AMPs killing bacteria is non-membrane damage intracellular targeting. It enters the cytosolic binds to specific targets, which inhibit the replication of genetic material and inhibit protein synthesis, inhibit cell wall synthesis, and reduces enzyme activity (Zhang et al. 2019). The AMPs depend on the electrostatic attraction to trigger their interaction with the bacterial membrane.

Recently, studies have shown that some AMPs not only have antibacterial effect, but also kill the cancerous cells. For example, R2PLx acquisition from pickerel frog can reduce the proliferation of prostate cancer cells PC-3 (Chen et al. 2018). Antimicrobial peptides θ-defensins show potential for application in breast cancer cell lines SKBR3 and MDA-MB-231, while it showed low toxicity to the normal human mammary epithelial HB2 (Strzelecka et al. 2017).

The normal cell membrane in an overall neutral charge. On the contrary, tumor cell membrane surface overexpression of the phosphatidylserine (PS), glycosylation modified protein, sialic acid protein, and O-glycosylated mucin, which makes tumor cells have high negative charges (Otvos 2017; Boohaker et al. 2012). The negative charge lead tumor cell interact with AMPs more sensitive rather than normal cell (Slaninová et al. 2012). The mechanism of AMPs on bacterial and tumor cell have been believed to share a similarity for membrane disturbance. AMPs exhibit cytotoxic effect on tumor cell by dissolving cell membranes and enter cell then bind to the target, inhibit tumor cell proliferation and induce apoptosis (Gera et al. 1991; Ouyang et al. 2002). In addition, in vivo studies have shown that AMPs can inhibit the growth of solid tumor, reduce the migration and invasion of cancer cells via regulating tumor angiogenesis (Wu et al. 2015).

In recent years, AMPs have received increasingly attention due to their exhibit potential on drug resistance and lower toxicity. Some AMPs shown broad-spectrum cytotoxic activity against bacteria and cancer cells, but harmless to normal cells (Hoskin et al. 2002). The peptide CC34 was selected through bioinformatic analysis using musca domestica antimicrobial peptide (Md-Cec) and Rana Chensinensis antimicrobial peptide (Chensirin) as parent peptides. Previous work shown CC34 has good thermal, pH and enzyme stability. However, the activities of antimicrobial peptides CC34 on cancer and the underlying mechanism were never reported. Therefore, the aimed of our study was to investigate the effect of CC34 against the SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cancer cells, and its potential mechanisms on antiproliferation and induce apoptosis.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: CC34 (GWLKKIGKKIERVGQHTRDAILPILSLIGGLLGK) was synthesized by Taopu Biotechnology Company (Shanghai, China). The purity of the antimicrobial peptide was higher than 95%, molecular mass was 3709.51 Da, as determined by high performance liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry (MS). Mueller-Hinton (MH) broth, Luria–Bertani (LB) medium, and PBS and Triton-100 were purchased from AOBOX Biothechnology (Beijing, China). RPMI 1640 medium, fetal bovine serum, penicillin-streptomycin, trypsin without EDTA solution bought from Hyclon (Logan, Utah, USA). Reactive Oxygen Species, Caspase-9, Caspase-3, ATP Assay Kit were purchased from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (Nanjing, China). Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit and Cell Cycle Assay Kit were purchased from Beijing 4 A Biotech Company (Beijing, China). Cell Mitochondria Isolation Kit, Whole Protein Extraction Kit, BCA Protein Assay Kit and Enhanced Chemiluminescence (ECL) Kit and HRP-conjugated secondary antibody were purchased from Institute of Biotechnology Beyotime (Shanghai, China). The primary antibodies against Cyt c, Bax, Bcl-2, COX IV and β-actin were all from Cell Signaling Technology (Danvers, MA, USA). Polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) was bought from Merck Millipore (Billerica, USA).

sec.title: Bacterial strains
sec.p: The Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC9027), Escherichia coli (ATCC29522), Enterobacter aerogenes (ATCC13048), Streptococcus faecalis (ATCC29212), Streptococcus agalactiae (ATCC13813), and Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC43300), all from the China General Microbiological Culture Collection Center (CGMCC).

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells were purchased from the National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures (Shanghai, China). Cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin-streptomycin solution at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator.

sec.title: Minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimal bactericidal concentration (MBC)
sec.p: To determine the MIC, a broth microdilution assay in 96-well microtiter plates was conducted by following the broth microdilution guideline of Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) (NCCLS. 2024). The bacterial concentration was diluted to approximately 105 CFU/mL, and twofold serial dilutions of CC34 (320 to 0.625 µg/mL) respectively 50 µL were added to the wells. Plates were incubated for 24 h at 37 °C. The MIC values were measured at 600 nm by microplate reader (Bio-Rad, iMark, USA).

The MBC was determined by plating 10 µL from each well with no visible turbidity in MH medium. After incubated at 37 °C overnight, the MBC was taken to be the least concentration able to prevent bacterial growth (Mataracı Kara et al. 2019).

sec.title: Bacterial biofilms quantification assay
sec.p: The effect of CC34 on the bacterial biofilm formation was determined by crystal violet staining method (Olson et al. 2018). The bacteria strains concentration of Escherichia coli and Streptococcus faecalis were diluted to the final concentration of 105 CFU/mL, and CC34 was diluted to final concentration of (2 × MIC to 1/16 × MIC). The 100 µL of bacterial suspensions and 100 µL of CC34 were placed into wells of sterile 96-well and wells with bacterial suspensions only were used as controls. Biofilms were allowed to grow at 37 °C for 24 h or 48 h without agitation. After incubation, the original culture were aspirated and the wells were washed twice with 200 µL PBS. To fix the biofilms, 200 µL of 99% methanol was added to the wells for 15 min and stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 30 min. Plates were washed by water and 100 µL of 30% acetic acid was added to each biofilm. The optical density was measured at 600 nm by microplate reader.

sec.title: NaCl permeability assay
sec.p: For CC34 NaCl permeability analysis, 100 µL of bacterial suspensions (105 CFU/mL) and peptide (final concentration of 1/2 × MIC) were added to 96-well plates. A final volume of 100 µL of NaCl solutions (200 to 80 mg/mL) was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 12 h (Hu et al. 2016). The wells with bacterial suspensions only were used as controls. The optical density at 600 nm was recorded.

sec.title: Hemolytic assay
sec.p: The hemolytic activities of CC34 were tested against chicken and mouse red blood cells (Stark et al. 2002). Freshly erythrocytes resuspended in PBS to create the 4% (vol/vol) red blood cell suspension. CC34 was diluted in PBS with concentrations ranging from 10 to 320 µg/mL, and 100 µL of the CC34 solution and 100 µL of the erythrocyte suspension were added to 96-well plates. After incubated for 1 h at 37 °C, the plates were determined by measuring the optical density at 492 nm. Erythrocyte treated with PBS and 0.1% Triton X-100 were used as agents for 0 and 100% hemolysis.

sec.title: Cell viability
sec.p: SGC-7901 or HepG-2 cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 104 cells/mL in 100 µL RPMI 1640 medium for 24 h. For the viability test, the original medium was discarded, and the cells were treated with serial dilutions of CC34 (100 µL/well) for 24 h. Then, aliquots of 10 µL MTT (5 mg/mL) were added to each well, and incubation was continued for 4 h. After aspirating the original culture solution, aliquots of 150 µL DMSO were added to each well, and the plate was placed on a shaker. The absorbance was measured at 492 nm, and the cells viability after treat-ment were calculated relative to the absorbance value of the control. RPMI 1640 was used as the negative control, and 5-Fu (10 µg/mL) was used as the positive control.

sec.title: Flow cytometry analysis for apoptosis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) and cell cycle
sec.p: SGC-7901 or HepG-2 cells (5 × 104 cells/well) in 6-well plates were incubated with CC34 for 24 h. Then, cells were harvested and stained with Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit in the dark. The percentage of apoptotic cells was analyzed using a flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, CytoFLEX, CA, USA).

Cell cycle analysis was assessed by Cell Cycle Assay Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, after peptides treatment of 24 h, cells were harvested by trypsin. Cells (4 × 106 cells /mL) were washed in PBS before resuspending the pellet in 250 µL of PBS. Added in 750 µL of ice-cold 100% ethanol and stored at 4 °C for 12 h. The cells were centrifuged for 5 min at 1000 rpm before washed in PBS. The cell pellet was resuspended in 50 µL of PBS, then 20 µLof Rnase A was added and stained with 400 µLof PI for 30 min in the dark. The cell cycle was determined using a flow cytometer.

Intracellular ROS were determined by a Reactive Oxygen Species Assay Kit. The cells were treated with CC34 for 24 h, then 10 µM DCFH-DA detection reagent was added to each sample suspension. The samples were incubation for 40 min at 37 °C in the dark, and data acquisition was carried out using the flow cytometer.

sec.title: Caspase activation and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) quantification analysis
sec.p: The activity of caspase enzymes in SGC-7901 or HepG-2 cells were assessed using the caspase-3 and − 9 Activity Assays Kit in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. The absorbance of each cell lysates sample was recorded using amicroplate reader at 405 nm.

The effects of CC34 on tumor intracellular ATP accumulation was assessed using an ATP Assay Kit. The cells were treated with concentrations of peptides for 24 h, then the cells centrifuged at 3000 rpm at 4˚C for 5 min. Cells were collected and lysed on ice, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm, 4˚C for 15 min. The supernatants were retained and the protein contents were quantify using a BCA Protein Assay Kit. ATP content was analyzed by spectrophotometer at 636 nm, and according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Western blot
sec.p: Total protein extraction was done for SGC-7901 cells treated with CC34 for 24 h by Whole Protein Extraction Kit. Mitochondrial fractions extracted was obtained with the Cell Mitochondria Isolation Kit. The protein content of the samples were measured using a BCA Protein Assay Kit. The proteins (30 µg) were separated by 12% SDS-PAGE and electrotransferred noto PVDF membranes. After blocking with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) at 37 °C for 2 h, each membrane was incubated with primary antibody Cyt c (1:1000), Bax (1:1000), Bcl-2 (1:1000), COX IV (1:1000) and β-actin (1:1000) at 4 °C overnight. The membranes were then washed for 5 min with TBST for 4 times. The membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (goat anti-rabbit, 3:5000) for 1 h at room temperature. Detection of the specific protein bands were performed using an ECL kit, and band densities were quantified using a gel imaging system (Bio-Rad, GelDoc XR, USA).

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: All the experiments were performed at least three times in triplicate, and data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Data analysis by one-way ANOVA was performed using SPSS 19.0, and P values of less than 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.

sec.title: Antimicrobial activity
sec.p: The antibacterial efficacy of the CC34 was evaluated by measuring its minimal inhibitory concentrations and minimal bactericidal concentrations. As shown in in Table 1, MIC values resulted between 20 and 160 µg/mL of peptides, while MBC values between 80 and > 320 µg/mL. The results demonstrated that CC34 performed higher antimicrobial activities against both Gram-negative bacteria and Gram-positive bacteria.

caption.p: Antibacterial activity and bactericidal activity of antimicrobial peptides CC34

sec.title: CC34 inhibited biofilms formation
sec.p: As shown in Fig. 1a, CC34 at a concentration of 2 × MIC, 1 × MIC, 1/2 × MIC, 1/4 × MIC significantly inhibited the formation of biofilms of Escherichia coli in 24 h (P < 0.01), at the same concentration of peptides could significantly reduced the formation of biofilms in 48 h (P < 0.01). Streptococcus faecalis biofilms formation were significantly inhibited at the concentration of 1/16 × MIC in 24 h and in 48 h (Fig. 1b). Biofilm formation was enhanced with the reduce of the concentration of CC34, and in a time-dependent manner.

caption.p: (a) Effects of CC34 on bacterial biofilm of E.coli. (b) Effects of CC34 on bacterial biofilm of S.faecalis. (c) Effects of CC34 on NaCl permeability of E.coli. (d) Effects of CC34 on NaCl permeability of S.faecalis. (e) Hemolytic activities of CC34 in chicken and mouse erythrocytes. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). The differences between the groups were assessed using ANOVA followed by Duncan’s test. Compared to control: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01

sec.title: NaCl permeability assay
sec.p: We investigated effects of CC34 on NaCl permeability of Escherichia coli and Streptococcus faecalis. The results of these tests were shown in Fig. 1c, d. Our results showed that the absorbance values of two strains reduced with the increased concentration of NaCl solution in the control group, and reached the lowest point at 160 and 140 µg/mL, respectively. Peptides reduced the values of OD600 of two strains and reached to their minimum values at concentration of 140 and 120 µg/mL.

sec.title: Hemolytic activity
sec.p: The hemolytic activity of CC34 was investigated on mouse and chicken red blood cells. As shown in Fig. 1e, the hemolysis of peptides against mouse and chicken erythrocytes were 19.22% and 12.65% at the concentration of 320 µg/mL. This concentration is much higher than the MIC values for all the determined strains, CC34 can exhibit low toxicity.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity of CC34 against cancer cells
sec.p: MTT assay was performed to identify the cytotoxicity of peptides in SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells. Figure 2 shows that CC34 significantly suppressed activity of SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells in a concentration-dependent manner. The Half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of peptides on SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells were 45.26 ± 0.12 and 25.24 ± 0.11 µg/mL, respectively.

caption.p: Cytotoxicity of CC34 in (a) SGC-7901 and (b) HepG-2 cells. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). The differences between the groups were assessed using ANOVA followed by Duncan’s test. Compared to control: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01

sec.title: Effects of CC34 on apoptosis, cell cycle and ROS generation
sec.p: To investigate whether CC34 induced apoptosis in SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells, we performed a double annexin V-FITC/PI staining assay (Fig. 3). Peptides treatment-induced apoptosis significantly in SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells in a dose-dependent manner.

caption.p: Effects of CC34 on inducing apoptosis of (a) SGC-7901 and (b) HepG-2 cells. Apoptotic cell death was measured by Annexin V/PI double staining. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). The differences between the groups were assessed using ANOVA followed by Duncan’s test. Compared to control: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01

sec.p: After treatment of SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells with CC34 for 24 h, CC34 induced a significant accumulation of cells in G0/G1 phase (Fig. 4). CC34 treatment-induced G0/G1 cell cycle arrests significantly in SGC-7901 cells (62.21%) compared to control cells (46.44%), while peptides treatment HepG-2 resulted in cell accumulation in G0/G1 phase (75.14%) compared to control (46.47%).

caption.p: CC34 induces the cell cycle arrest in (a) SGC-7901 and (b) HepG-2 cells. Cells were treated with CC34 for 24 h, stained with PI and analyzed by flow cytometry. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). The differences between the groups were assessed using ANOVA followed by Duncan’s test. Compared to control: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01

sec.p: For investigating the ROS-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis effects of CC34, we assessed the accumulation of cellular ROS in the cancer cells (Fig. 5). The results showed that SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells were treated with CC34 in 11.25–6.25 µg/mL for 24 h, ROS generation were markedly increased in a dose-dependent manner.

caption.p: Production of ROS in (a) SGC-7901 and (b) HepG-2 cells after treating with CC34 for 24 h. ROS levels were measured using the flow cytometry. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). The differences between the groups were assessed using ANOVA followed by Duncan’s test. Compared to control: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01

sec.title: Effects of CC34 on caspase activity and cellular ATP levels
sec.p: The enzymatic activities of the caspases-9 and − 3 in SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells treated with or without peptides were estimated to understand the role of CC34 induction of apoptosis via mitochondrial pathway. Results in Fig. 6a and b showed significantly induction of both caspase-9 and − 3 after treatment of cancer cells with CC34. Further on, to observe the effects of CC34 on mitochondrial, cellular ATP levels were determined. As indicated in Fig. 6c, accumulation ATP levels in both cells treated with or without CC34 were reduced in a dose-dependent manner.

caption.p: Caspase-3 (a) and − 9 (b) activity and cellular ATP levels (c) in cancer cells after treating with CC34 for 24 h. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). The differences between the groups were assessed using ANOVA followed by Duncan’s test. Compared to control: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01

sec.title: Effects of CC34 on the expression of apoptosis-associated proteins in SGC-7901cells
sec.p: Western blot analysis was used to evaluate the induction effects of CC34 on the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. As shown in Fig. 7 the expression levels of pro-apoptotic protein Bax in SGC-7901 cells treated with CC34 significantly high, while antiapoptotic protein Bcl-2 were reduced. Moreover, treatment with CC34 increased expression of Cyt c in cytosol, but decreased the expression of Cyt c in mitochondria, thus changed the intracellular distribution of Cyt c.

caption.p: Representative images of Western blotting for Bax, Bcl-2, Cyt c, COX IV and β-actin in SGC- 7901 cells treated with CC34 for 24 h (a). Each bar graph presents the densitometric quantification of the Western blotting bands (b). Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). The differences between the groups were assessed using ANOVA followed by Duncan’s test. Compared to control: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In a previous study by our lab, we tried to design six antimicrobial peptides by increasing positively charged and hydrophobic properties on Cec Md and Chensirin as the template (Sun 2010). After hemolytic activity, cytotoxicity in RAW264.7 cells and stability in different temperatures and pH tests, we have obtained antimicrobial peptide CC34, emerged potential biological activity and stability but low toxicity. Antibiotics have been the most powerful weapon against deleterious infections, since it been discovered. However, drug-resistant is a serious challenges for public health (Li et al. 2020a, b). Due to the generous positive charges on the surface of molecules, AMPs were potentially unique bactericidal mechanism, which limited this defect (Maselli et al. 2020). Antimicrobial peptide CC34 a highly cationic (5.5+) peptide with the potential for therapeutic applications.

Our results demonstrate that CC34 exhibited the strong activity against Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. The results were similar with the AMPs reported before (Theansungnoen et al. 2016; Koehbach et al. 2021). Biofilm was defined as a polymeric matrix by self-produced extra surface within the bacterial community, changed markedly in beneficial to exogenous stress tolerance and caused most resistance against medicine (Sahoo et al. 2021). Promoting the dispersion of biofilms and inhibiting their formation is a new research direction. In this work, we report that CC34 could inhibit the formation of both Gram-negative bacteria and Gram-positive bacteria biofilms and obviously change the permeability of bacteria. AMPs depending on their positive charge and unique secondary structure to effectively attracted to bacteria and biofilm sites, revealing antibiofilm properties (Kalsy et al. 2020; Krishnan et al. 2020; Memariani et al. 2018). High toxicity especially hemolysis is constantly an obstacle to the application of AMPs (Grafskaia et al. 2019). In our study, CC34 exhibited low hemolytic and cytotoxic activities.

AMPs not only have a strong bactericidal activity, but also show a significant anticancer activity, which is attributed to the mutual attraction with the negatively charged membrane (Burdukiewicz et al. 2020; Deslouches and Di 2017). Therefore, the aim of this study was to investigate the effect of CC34 on cancer cells. As expected, peptide could inhibit the proliferation of SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells. Further studies to determine the mechanism of CC34 significantly reduce in cells proliferation, we assessed apoptosis, cell cycle, ROS generation, caspase activity, cellular ATP levels, expression of apoptosis-associated proteinsin in cancer cells by peptide demonstrated. Cell cycle plays a crucial role in both cell proliferation and apoptosis. CC34 blocked cell cycle at G0/G1 phase in SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells. The result of ours correlated with previous studies that AMPs could induce cancer cell cycle arrest (Kuroda et al. 2017; Ma et al. 2016).

The apoptotic pathway is mainly involved in the death receptor pathway and mitochondrial pathway. The mitochondrial pathway is plays a key role in cancer inhibition and it is the target of anticancer research. AMPs induced apoptosis through the mitochondrial pathway and ROS accumulation in cancer cells (Xia et al. 2016; Cerón et al. 2010). Our results showed that CC34 significantly induced cells apoptosis and ROS generation in SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells. ROS is mainly produced in mitochondria and accumulation of ROS may lead to cell damage.The excess ROS production can induce cancer cell death through triggering mitochondrial-mediated apoptotic pathway (Tülüce et al. 2017). In mitochondrial-mediated apoptotic pathway, the increase of pro-apoptotic protein Bax, Cyt c in cytosol, the decrease of anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2, Cyt c in mitochondria and activates caspase-9 as a downstream target. This process ultimately induces activation of the effector caspase-3 (Losuwannarak et al. 2018). Our results for the activities of caspase-3, -9 assay suggest that CC34 treatment prompted the activities of caspase in cancer cells. A higher Bax/Bcl-2 ratio may lead to the release of Cyt c from mitochondria into cytosol (Liu et al. 2011). Accumulation of cyt c in the cytosol could activate caspase-9, -3 and contribute to cell apoptosis (Esmaeili et al. 2016). The decrease of mitochondrial membrane potential, decrease of ATP synthesis, and the increase of mitochondrial membrane permeability are favours apoptosis (Li et al. 2020a, b). The results of the present study revealed that CC34 treatment suppressed the ATP generation in the SGC-7901 and HepG-2 cells. Moreover, CC34 treatment strikingly reduced Bcl-2 and Cyt c (mitochondria) expression in SGC-7901 cells, whereas Bax and Cyt c (cytosol) expression were increased. These data confirm that CC34-induced apoptosis by the mitochondrial pathway.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In summary, evidence from this investigation demonstrates that antimicrobial peptide CC34 has an effectively antimicrobial and bactericidal activities with low hemolysis and toxicity. CC34 has not only exhibited the performed potent antibacterial activities but also revealed strong anticancer activities. CC34 suppressed cancer cells viability via inducing cell-cycle arrest and mitochondria-mediated apoptosis, through induced the upregulation of the ROS generation, the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, cytochrome C release and caspase-9, -3 activation. Therefore, CC34 is a potential candidate for novel clinical applications in antimicrobial and antitumor.
